lines: A team sets up a compacted topic expecting the old value for a key to vanish the instant the new one lands.
A full day goes by, and someone notices the old value is still sitting right there, perfectly readable.
That's not a bug slipping through — it's exactly what the settings they configured actually promise, once you read them closely.
Picture the same strip of data this chapter has been building all along.
Now put two completely different rules on top of it for deciding what gets to stay.
One throws away whatever's old enough. The other keeps only the newest value for each key, no matter how old it is.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Time-based retention eventually throws old data away. The question is what unit it actually operates on.
Does it ever reach in and remove one specific record the moment that record ages out, or does it always act on something bigger?
answer: It always acts on something bigger: a whole segment, never a single record plucked out of the middle of one.
A segment only gets deleted once every record inside it, down to the newest one, has aged past the retention window.
That's a direct consequence of how a segment lives on disk in the first place — you can't quietly carve one record out of a file without rewriting the whole thing.

lines: Here's that rule, measured on three real segments.
One whose newest record is still fresh enough survives completely untouched.
One whose newest record has aged past the window gets deleted in its entirety — not trimmed, not partially cleaned, just gone, all at once.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
Compaction exists to drop records once a newer value for the same key shows up.
Does the cleaner rewrite the log the instant that happens, or does it hold off for some condition first?
answer: Rewriting an entire log every single time one record gets superseded would mean constant, wasteful work for almost no benefit.
So the cleaner waits until enough of the log has gone stale — crossing a configured fraction — before it bothers doing any work at all.

lines: Here's that exact gauge, measured in both states.
Below the configured threshold, the cleaner simply does nothing. It's not lazy — it's waiting on purpose.
Cross that threshold, and a cleaning pass actually fires.
That threshold isn't the only thing in play, though — there's also a floor and a ceiling on timing.
A record that's too fresh stays protected no matter how dirty the log has gotten around it.
A record that's old enough gets forced into eligibility regardless of that same ratio — only the stretch in between actually depends on it.
A delete itself doesn't last forever either — it has its own built-in expiration.
A consumer that catches up to the front of the log quickly enough sees that delete marker and knows the key is gone.
A consumer that's still lagging once that marker's own window closes can miss the deletion completely — the key just quietly stops showing up as deleted at all.
Every number in this reel so far came from one real run of this topic's own toy retention and compaction model, happening just now.
The segment check, deciding exactly what got kept and what got dropped whole.
The dirty-ratio gate, the lag window's floor and ceiling, and both tombstone outcomes, side by side.
So: deletion by age always acts on a whole segment, never a single record.
Compaction waits for a dirty-ratio gate, bounded underneath by a floor and above by a ceiling.
And a tombstone runs on its own clock entirely — which is exactly what makes calling a compacted topic a changelog a precise claim, not just a loose comparison.
